meta.title: Who really said "When I was a boy of fourteen, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be twenty-one, I was astonished at how much the old man had learned in seven years"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Mark Twain almost certainly never said it. The line first appears in 1915, five years after his death, and no version exists in his works.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When I was a boy of fourteen, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be twenty-one, I was astonished at how much the old man had learned in seven years'?
meta.ogDescription: An apocryphal saying pinned on Twain since 1915. Not in any of his works, and his father died when he was eleven — making the premise impossible.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — an apocryphal saying
answer.authorDates: Attributed to Mark Twain (1835–1910) only from 1915 onward
answer.sourceLine: This crowd-pleaser is one of the internet’s most durable fake Twain quotes. It appears in none of his books, letters, or notebooks; the earliest known version surfaces in December 1915 — five years after his death — and Twain’s own father died when Samuel was eleven, so the fourteen-to-twenty-one setup could never have been autobiographical. No genuine author has ever been found.

source.excerpt: When I was a boy of fourteen, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be twenty-one, I was astonished at how much the old man had learned in seven years.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest attribution to The Square Deal (December 1915), five years after Twain’s death, and finds no direct evidence connecting Twain to the saying.
Wikiquote ↗ files the line as unsourced, noting it is “not found in Twain’s works” and that his father died when Twain was eleven.
Early citations vary the ages considerably (fourteen–twenty-one, seventeen–twenty-five, seventeen–twenty-seven), and the modern wording was fixed by a September 1937 Reader’s Digest ↗ printing.
No genuine originator has ever been identified — it circulates as an anonymous folk aphorism attached to Twain’s name.
source.excerptNote: The wording above (starting age fourteen, ending age twenty-one) is the popular modern form, standardized by a September 1937 Reader’s Digest printing. Earlier citations from 1915–1931 give wildly different ages — seventeen to twenty-five, seventeen to twenty-seven — a classic sign of a saying that grew in the retelling rather than a fixed quotation from a real text.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording cannot be tied to any identifiable author or first-publication work — it is an anonymous saying misattributed to Mark Twain, first recorded in 1915. With no sourced work and no known author, no copyright or public-domain status can honestly be asserted.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: About the name on the quote
author.metaLine: 1835–1910 · American author & humorist (pen name of Samuel L. Clemens)
author.bio: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens, author of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and one of the most quoted — and misquoted — writers in the English language. His reputation as a plain-spoken wit makes him a magnet for feel-good aphorisms he never wrote. This father-and-son line is one of them: it appears nowhere in his verified writing, and his own father died when Clemens was eleven, so the story could not have been his.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook fake-Twain quote: a warm, quotable observation about growing up, welded to the era’s most bankable humorist long after he could object.

items.why: The saying is not found in any of Twain’s books, letters, or notebooks. The first known attribution to him appears in The Square Deal in December 1915 — five years after his 1910 death — and Quote Investigator ↗ finds no direct evidence tying him to it.
The quote pivots on the narrator’s father being present from age fourteen to twenty-one. Wikiquote ↗ notes Twain’s father died when Twain was eleven, so the line cannot describe his real life.

items.who: A saying that grew in retelling
items.why: Early printings give different ages — seventeen to twenty-five, seventeen to twenty-seven — before a September 1937 Reader’s Digest version fixed the now-standard “fourteen…twenty-one.” Fixed quotations don’t drift like this; folklore does.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: an anonymous aphorism, first recorded in 1915, that was attached to Twain’s name and never left. No genuine author has been identified ↗.

context.heading: Why the line sticks to Twain
lead: The sentiment — that a father grows wiser precisely as the son grows up — is old and widespread, and versions of the joke circulated in the 1910s and 1920s without a fixed author. Twain’s name gave it authority and a punch-line cadence, and once Reader’s Digest printed the tidy fourteen-to-twenty-one form in the late 1930s, that wording became the canonical “Twain” quote.

It endures because it is genuinely good — self-deprecating, generous to parents, and exactly the sort of thing Twain might have said. That plausibility is the whole problem: it is why the misattribution has survived a century of fact-checking.
context.pull: Fixed quotations don’t drift in wording. Folklore does — and this one drifted for two decades before settling on Twain.
